channel.title: Daily Recap — 🚀 Space News
channel.description: What happened in 🚀 Space News, recapped daily from subscribed feeds.

item.title: Pentagon eyes military satellites around the Moon
item.description:
The Department of the Air Force is asking industry whether it could put up to five military satellites into cislunar space — the vast region between Earth and the Moon — with spacecraft ready to launch by late 2029 and initial operations in 2031. The November 2 request for information describes the satellites as "seed vehicles" that would inform an acquisition strategy for a future proliferated cislunar constellation, and responses are due November 24.

The notice names no mission and no specific orbit, and the Air Force calls itself only "notionally interested" — early market research, not a funded program. Officials have said they want space domain awareness, positioning and navigation, and communications far beyond geostationary orbit. The push is driven by China's plan to land astronauts on the Moon by 2030, and follows pathfinders like the Air Force Research Laboratory's $75 million Oracle-M mission, due to launch in mid-2027.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: Pentagon mulls placing fleet of military satellites around the Moon

item.title: New Democratic Congress likely to defund and rename Golden Dome
item.description:
After Democrats won both chambers in the November 3 midterms, President Trump's Golden Dome missile defense program looks set for a major overhaul when the new Congress is seated in January. With two top Republican backers leaving Congress, Democrats are expected to write the Pentagon budget, impose funding limits, and strip out the most controversial piece: space-based interceptors meant to shoot down missiles during their boost phase.

Military officials have already signaled they may backpedal on the boost-phase capability, and the program will almost certainly be renamed — "There's no doubt that whatever it's going to be called, it won't be called Golden Dome," one analyst said. But this isn't wholesale cancellation: much of Golden Dome predates Trump's January 2025 executive order, which consolidated existing missile defense efforts, and the expectation is a scaled-back program rather than throwing the baby out with the bathwater. The $17 billion Golden Dome fund in the pending reconciliation bill now looks dead.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: New Democratic Congress will likely strip the gilding from Trump's Golden Dome

item.title: SpaceX now calls itself an "infrastructure company"
item.description:
SpaceX's vice president of launch, Kiko Dontchev, told last week's UP.Summit conference in Florida that the company has fundamentally changed. "In the last couple years, when I talk about SpaceX, yes, we are a rocket company, but fundamentally we are an infrastructure company at this point," he said. "We're building infrastructure on the ground and low Earth orbit, soon on the Moon, and obviously eventually Mars."

Dontchev also described sharply accelerating AI adoption this year, especially after integrating tools from xAI — the Musk-founded AI company SpaceX acquired earlier this year — with tasks that once took hours or days now taking seconds to minutes. He also confirmed the Falcon 9, which has dominated global launch for a decade, is on the road to retirement as Starship takes over.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: SpaceX now fundamentally an "infrastructure company," senior official says

item.title: Chandra solves a 15-year mystery: a star that keeps faking its own death
item.description:
Using NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory, astronomers have finally explained a giant star that has been erupting like a supernova — without ever dying — for 15 years. The star, AT 2016blu, is a luminous blue variable more than 33 times the Sun's mass in the galaxy NGC 4559, 30 million light-years away. Since 2012 it has flared at least 27 times, roughly every 113 days, with supernova-like bursts.

A study in The Astrophysical Journal reveals the cause: a previously hidden companion — a stellar-mass black hole or a neutron star — that pulls material off the giant star at their closest approach in an oval orbit. The stolen gas heats until it shines brightly in X-rays; Chandra data from March 2026 showed the system over 100 times brighter in X-rays than in 2001–2002, before the outbursts began. It's the first X-ray detection of this class of erupting star, and it may link these "supernova impostors" to the mysterious ultra-luminous X-ray sources.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA's Chandra Finds Source of Star's Mysterious Outbursts

item.title: Perseverance finds ruby-like minerals — and bags its first sample in over a year
item.description:
Two new NASA blog posts from Perseverance's team in Jezero Crater tell a story of unexpected geology and hard-won persistence. Using SuperCam's time-resolved luminescence, the rover detected chromium atoms locked inside corundum — the mineral whose gemstone form is ruby. Corundum is a metamorphic mineral that shouldn't exist on a planet without plate tectonics, but large asteroid impacts can create local metamorphism through long-term heating — and Perseverance is exploring very ancient terrain near Jezero's rim. The findings were published in Geophysical Research Letters earlier this year.

Perseverance also collected its first sample in more than a year. Its latest abrasion, "Pumbe," resembled an earlier rock, "Badger Peak" — a gabbro so hard the drill couldn't core it. The team drove about 100 meters to similar light-toned rock, chose a flatter target and a less-worn bit, and drilled 3.1 centimeters in. The resulting sample, "Singita," may be among the oldest rocks in the rover's collection, likely formed deep in the crust and excavated by one or more large impacts.

Sources

  • NASA: Rubies on Mars?
  • NASA: Newest Sample, Oldest Rock?

item.title: Curiosity drills its 49th hole, then takes a breather to recharge
item.description:
NASA's Curiosity rover has drilled its 49th hole on Mars. During sols 5050–5055, the rover returned to an area where it had found disc-shaped inclusions in the rocks — possibly crystals — and drilled a sample dubbed "Nazca" to investigate them. The team is still analyzing the inclusions, but the site was chosen to follow up on the intriguing shapes spotted earlier.

After the drilling campaign, Curiosity spent sols 5056–5062 largely recharging its batteries before returning to normal drilling activities. The rover, which landed in Gale Crater in 2012 and is now in its 14th year of operations, continues to work through a planned science campaign, with the recharge sols a routine part of managing power on the aging but still healthy spacecraft.

Sources

  • NASA: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5050-5055: It's Nazca, Our 49th Drill Hole
  • NASA: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5056-5062: Charging Back Up!

item.title: NASA opens applications for its next astronaut class
item.description:
NASA has opened applications for its next class of astronauts, who will join the agency as the United States returns to the Moon. The new class will train for missions that could include lunar surface expeditions under Artemis as well as long-duration stays aboard the International Space Station, and eventually missions deeper into space.

NASA selects astronauts only every few years — the last class was announced in 2021 — and thousands of applicants typically compete for roughly a dozen spots. The announcement frames the class as the explorers who will write the next chapter of human spaceflight, arriving at a moment when the agency's crewed ambitions are shifting decisively from low Earth orbit back toward the Moon.

Sources

  • NASA: La NASA busca a la próxima generación de astronautas

item.title: NASA puts up $1 million for students to design a Moon Base
item.description:
NASA announced the opening of its $1 million Moon Base Student Challenge on Sunday during a MAX POWER event at Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida. The competition invites teams of U.S. high school and post-secondary students to contribute designs for a Moon Base, framed as part of a "Golden Age of Science."

It's a modest but meaningful piece of the Artemis-era push: getting students to think seriously about lunar habitation — the structures, systems, and logistics a permanent base would need — while building a pipeline of future engineers. Details on the competition's phases and prizes are available through NASA's announcement.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Announces $1 Million to Students for Moon Base Challenge

item.title: NASA funds Moon Base transport, nuclear rover, and surface infrastructure
item.description:
NASA announced a suite of awards on Saturday to expand its Moon Base exploration, science, and infrastructure capabilities, as the agency works with American industry to establish a sustained presence on the Moon. The investments cover commercial robotic deliveries, a nuclear-powered rover named PROMISE, launch and orbital transfer services, and surface infrastructure.

The package is a concrete step from one-off landings toward a permanent lunar presence: nuclear power would let rovers operate through the two-week lunar night, and the commercial delivery and transfer awards spread the logistics load across private partners. Watch for the individual award details and timelines as NASA releases them — the real test will be whether these pieces come together on schedule ahead of crewed landings.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Awards Moon Base Transportation, Technology, Science Projects

item.title: NASA opens applications for its next astronaut class
item.description:
NASA has opened applications for its next class of astronauts, the explorers who will fly as America returns to the Moon, builds the Moon Base, and lays the groundwork for the first crewed missions to Mars.

Astronaut selection is a rare, high-profile event — classes are chosen only every few years — and this one is explicitly tied to the lunar program rather than just station duty. The application window is now open; expect a long selection process, with the new class likely announced well over a year from now.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Seeks Next Generation of Explorers to Join Astronaut Corps

item.title: AST SpaceMobile is building its own heavy-lift rocket
item.description:
AST SpaceMobile, the company behind the Bluebird direct-to-cell satellite constellation, announced a $1.3 billion engine deal with Firefly Aerospace to power its own heavy-lift rocket, dubbed Blacklift. The company framed the rocket as the final piece of its vertical-integration strategy — controlling its own launch capacity rather than depending on a crowded commercial launch market.

The move underscores just how tight launch supply has become: a satellite operator is now willing to spend over a billion dollars to build its own rocket rather than wait in line. AST says Blacklift will significantly expand its total addressable market, suggesting the rocket could eventually serve customers beyond its own constellation. For now, the deal is a bet that launch scarcity is a long-term problem worth solving in-house.

Sources

  • Spaceflight Now: AST SpaceMobile unveils $1.3 billion engine deal with Firefly Aerospace to power new heavy-lift rocket
  • Space - Ars Technica: You know the launch market is tough when satellite companies start building rockets

item.title: Falcon 9 launches classified Space Force mission from Vandenberg
item.description:
A SpaceX Falcon 9 lifted off from pad 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California at 4:48 p.m. PST, carrying a classified payload for the U.S. Space Force. Details of the mission remain undisclosed, as is typical for national-security launches.

The payload is believed to be satellites based on SpaceX's Starshield platform, the company's military-focused variant of its Starlink satellite bus. The launch adds to a steady cadence of Space Force missions flying on Falcon 9, which has become the workhorse for U.S. national-security spaceflight.

Sources

  • Spaceflight Now: Falcon 9 launches from California on classified mission for U.S. Space Force

item.title: Rocket Report: Artemis II's fiery return, New Glenn slips again
item.description:
This week's Rocket Report leads with Artemis II, whose capsule tore through the atmosphere on its return — a dramatic reentry that put the Orion heat shield through its paces on the crewed lunar flyby mission. Meanwhile, Blue Origin's New Glenn won't fly this year, pushing the heavy-lift rocket's debut further back.

Elsewhere, China launched what amounts to a mini Falcon Heavy, and Japan's Interstellar Technologies announced more government funding for its Zero rocket. The picture is familiar: established programs are hitting milestones while next-generation heavy lifters keep slipping — and international competitors keep closing the gap.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: Rocket Report: Artemis II literally tore through the atmosphere; New Glenn delay

item.title: Blue Origin unveils a new third stage and a more powerful engine for New Glenn
item.description:
Blue Origin unveiled two major New Glenn upgrades at an invite-only event at Kennedy Space Center ahead of this weekend's NASA-backed Max Power airshow: a new third stage and a new first-stage engine.

The third stage, called Glenn Stage 3 (GS3), is designed for missions needing direct injection to geostationary orbit or Earth-escape trajectories — up to 14 metric tons to GEO and 20 metric tons to trans-lunar injection on the larger 9×4 vehicle. It's powered by the BE-7 engine from Blue Origin's lunar landers, and the company says a government mission to cislunar space is already lined up for 2028. Testing is underway in Texas, where a composite liquid-hydrogen tank passed pressure tests at 150% of its operating limit.

The new first-stage engine, Northstar, burns liquefied natural gas and liquid oxygen like the BE-4 but produces 715,000 pounds of thrust versus 640,000, and Blue Origin says it can be assembled in under a day thanks to manufacturing advances. It went from program approval to testing in just 11 months and will fly alongside the BE-4 on the 9×4 vehicle. The announcements come as the company works toward its return to flight following May's launchpad explosion.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: Blue Origin says it is building a higher-performing rocket engine at 1/4 the cost
  • Spaceflight Now: Blue Origin reveals new kick stage, engines for its New Glenn rockets

item.title: Spacewalkers finish five-year effort to upgrade the space station's power supply
item.description:
Spacewalking astronauts Joshua Kutryk and Anil Menon installed the eighth and final upgraded solar array on the International Space Station on Thursday, completing a five-year effort to modernize the station's power supply. The pair unfurled the last International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (IROSA), working through an unexpected power snag along the way.

The upgrade was essential to the station's future: the new arrays boost power generation enough to keep the orbiting lab running through its planned retirement in 2030, supporting both research and the growing roster of visiting commercial vehicles. Five years and eight spacewalks later, the station's power system is finally done — one of the last major upgrades before the ISS era winds down.

Sources

  • Spaceflight Now: Spacewalkers complete five-year effort to upgrade space station power supply
  • Spaceflight Now: As it happened: spacewalkers install space station’s eighth and final upgraded solar array

item.title: NASA Unveils the X-70 Fractal, a New Experimental Aircraft
item.description:
NASA unveiled its newest experimental aircraft, the X-70 Fractal, on Wednesday at the UP.Summit at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The crewed, high-performance research platform is designed to accelerate development and testing of advanced aviation technologies, with rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology that lets researchers try out new concepts far faster than building a new airframe each time.

The X-70 continues NASA's long X-plane tradition of using dedicated test aircraft to de-risk technologies before they reach commercial or military fleets. By making the flight controls themselves adaptable, NASA can explore a wider range of aerodynamic and control ideas on a single platform, potentially shortening the path from lab to runway for the next generation of aircraft.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Announces X-70 Experimental Aircraft to Advance Flight Research

item.title: NASA Lays Out Accelerated Artemis Plan: Americans Back on the Moon in 2028
item.description:
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and agency leaders shared the agency's accelerated path back to the lunar surface on October 23, targeting a crewed landing in 2028. The plan advances toward the Artemis III test flight in 2027 and the Artemis IV mission, compressing a schedule that had drifted under earlier plans.

The acceleration matters because the Moon program is effectively a race against China's own crewed lunar ambitions, and because Artemis is the testbed for the hardware and operations NASA wants to use for Mars. Hitting 2027 and 2028 will depend on the lunar lander, spacesuits, and Orion spacecraft all maturing on time — the same items that have slipped before, so the dates are a commitment to watch, not a guarantee.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Shares Plans to Accelerate Artemis, Return to Moon

item.title: Swift Observatory Burns Up Over Indonesia After 22 Years in Orbit
item.description:
NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory plunged back into Earth's atmosphere Wednesday over western Indonesia, ending nearly 22 years in orbit. The gamma-ray burst hunter had been a workhorse since 2004, rapidly slewing to catch the afterglows of the universe's most violent explosions and pinpointing them for telescopes around the world.

A rescue attempt to save the aging spacecraft failed, leaving reentry as the only option. Swift's legacy is a catalog of thousands of gamma-ray bursts and a fast-response model that shaped how modern time-domain astronomy works — when something flashes in the sky, the field now expects to know where it is within minutes, and Swift is a big reason why.

Sources

  • Spaceflight Now: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory reenters over Western Indonesia

item.title: After Texas' Blue Wave, What Happens to SpaceX?
item.description:
Elon Musk moved SpaceX to Texas in part for its business-friendly, Republican-led politics — and on Tuesday the state swung Democratic in a blue wave that flipped the governorship and a Senate seat. Ars Technica looks at what the political shift could mean for a company whose Starbase complex in South Texas and whose launch cadence depend heavily on state cooperation.

The practical impact is uncertain: much of SpaceX's regulatory relationship runs through federal agencies, not Austin, and Texas' space-friendly posture has had bipartisan support. But a new state government could revisit tax incentives, land-use decisions, and environmental oversight around Starbase. As one observer quoted in the piece put it, data centers in space are "looking pretty appealing right now" — a reminder that the company has options if the ground politics get complicated.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: After Texas' blue wave, what happens to Elon Musk and SpaceX?

item.title: NASA Awards Ka-Band Satellite Relay Contracts to Keep Missions Connected
item.description:
NASA selected three companies on Wednesday to develop Ka-band space relay capability concepts compatible with missions already in orbit, ensuring service continuity for existing spacecraft without requiring modifications to their onboard systems. The work aims at end-to-end solutions covering space, ground, launch, operations, and integration.

The awards are part of NASA's shift from owning its own relay satellites, like the aging Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System, toward buying communications as a commercial service. Ka-band offers far higher data rates than older frequencies, which matters as missions generate ever-larger volumes of science data — but the transition has to be seamless, since spacecraft already flying can't be retrofitted.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Announces Ka-Band Satellite Relay Awards for Space Communications

item.title: NASA Landing-Navigation Test Shows Promise for Future Moon Landings
item.description:
NASA successfully demonstrated technology designed to help spacecraft autonomously navigate to safe landing sites on the Moon and other planets. An Alta-X drone carrying the agency's SPLICE guidance, navigation, and control payload completed simulated lunar descent and landing maneuvers on August 27, using onboard sensing to pick a safe touchdown point in real time.

Autonomous hazard avoidance is a key gap for Artemis: the Moon's south pole, where NASA wants to land, is rugged and shadowed, and landing there safely without a pilot's eyes on the terrain requires the spacecraft to judge for itself. The drone test is a step toward proving SPLICE can do that job before it flies on a real lander.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Navigation Experiment Shows Promise for Planetary Landings

item.title: Hubble Finds Dwarf Galaxies Are Missing Oxygen They Should Have
item.description:
Researchers using NASA's Hubble Space Telescope studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies — small systems holding a few thousand to hundreds of millions of stars — and found that much of the oxygen they expected to see is missing. The finding, highlighted with a new image of the dwarf irregular galaxy NGC 4449 released November 2, is a genuine puzzle for models of how galaxies make and keep their chemical elements.

Oxygen is forged in massive stars and scattered by supernovae, so a galaxy's oxygen content is a record of its star-forming history. If dwarf galaxies are losing oxygen — perhaps blown out by supernova winds — or never made as much as models predict, astronomers will need to revise how the smallest galaxies evolve, and by extension how the chemical enrichment of the early universe worked.

Sources

  • NASA: Hubble Reveals Cosmic Mystery

item.title: NASA's Swift observatory to burn up this week after more than two decades in space
item.description:
NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is set to burn up in Earth's atmosphere this week, ending a mission that lasted more than two decades. As of Monday, the US Space Force predicted re-entry at approximately 3:30 a.m. EST on Wednesday, November 4, somewhere within about 21 degrees north or south of the equator — a band that is mostly ocean.

Swift spent its long career chasing gamma-ray bursts and other transient cosmic explosions, becoming one of astronomy's most productive workhorses. Its uncontrolled but low-risk re-entry marks the quiet end of an era: the observatory outlived its design life many times over, and its demise is a reminder of how much of our astrophysics infrastructure is aging at once.

Sources

  • Spaceflight Now: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory to burn up this week after more than two decades in space

item.title: One space company is betting its future on a propellant available everywhere
item.description:
A space company is betting its future on a propellant that is available just about everywhere — water. The pitch is straightforward: if your spacecraft runs on something you can find across the solar system, you don't have to carry all your fuel from Earth, and refueling stops being a distant dream.

Water as propellant would reshape mission economics, especially for spacecraft that need to maneuver long after launch. The bet is still a bet — the engineering has to prove out — but the logic is compelling enough that a company is willing to stake its future on it, and the idea of in-space resources moving from theory to business plan is itself a milestone.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: This space company is betting its future on a propellant available everywhere

item.title: Spacewalkers install a new solar array on the space station
item.description:
Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk was photographed during the October 29 spacewalk, with the International Space Station soaring 267 miles above the South Atlantic Ocean. Kutryk and NASA astronaut Anil Menon installed a new roll-out solar array on the station and completed some get-ahead work for future tasks.

Roll-out arrays are the station's ongoing power upgrade, replacing aging panels with lighter, more efficient ones that keep the orbiting lab running as it ages. The image is a vivid reminder that the station's longevity depends on regular, hands-on maintenance in one of the harshest workplaces imaginable.

Sources

  • NASA: Astronaut and Earth

item.title: NASA astronaut and STEM creator to beam into classrooms live from the station
item.description:
Students across the country will get a live, interactive in-flight call with the International Space Station, featuring NASA astronaut Anil Menon and STEM creator Mark Rober, founder of the ClassCrunchLabs Foundation. Hosted by NASA's Office of STEM Engagement, the event celebrates National STEM Day by bringing real-world science directly into classrooms.

Pairing a working astronaut with one of the internet's most popular science communicators is a deliberate play for young attention: the goal is to make space science feel immediate and reachable, not distant. For students watching, the takeaway is simple — the people doing this work were once sitting in classrooms just like theirs.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Astronaut, STEM Creator Connect with Students for STEM Day

item.title: The Pacific's busy storm season, seen from orbit
item.description:
Earth-observing satellites captured a notably busy Pacific storm season, including Super Typhoon In-fa, which developed an unusually large eye, and the remnants of Typhoon Champi, which transitioned into an extratropical storm targeting Alaska. The imagery shows storms evolving across vast ocean distances before they ever threaten land.

Beyond the spectacle, the season is a case study in why orbital observation matters: tracking a storm's structure and evolution from space gives forecasters the lead time that saves lives. In-fa's oversized eye and Champi's long journey to Alaska both illustrate how Pacific systems can stay dangerous far beyond their tropical origins.

Sources

  • NASA: The Pacific’s Busy Storm Season
